known_pitfalls.symptom: The SessionStart hooks silently do not run: no HANDOFF reload and no methodology warning.
known_pitfalls.cause: Since Claude Code 2.1.139, on Windows it uses the native PowerShell tool; without Git for Windows there is no `bash` on the machine.
known_pitfalls.action: Install Git for Windows, then: git config --global core.autocrlf input

known_pitfalls.when: Windows, the first prompt after installing/updating claude-mem
known_pitfalls.symptom: 'UserPromptSubmit hook timed out after 60s', slow session startup, then later 'UserPromptSubmit operation blocked by hook: claude-mem worker unreachable for 6 consecutive hooks' — the latter STOPS the work, no prompt can be submitted.
known_pitfalls.cause: TWO different failures, do not mix them up. (1) ON FIRST RUN: claude-mem's bun-runner.js downloads and installs the Bun runtime (https://bun.sh); from a cold start this exceeds the hook's 60 s limit — that is the 'timed out after 60s'. (2) PERSISTENTLY, on Windows: the worker communicates over a Unix socket (.sock), which does not work on Windows — that is the 'worker unreachable'. Installing Bun does NOT solve (2): on 2026-09-02 Bun was present on the laptop (~/.bun/bin/bun), yet the worker stayed unreachable.
known_pitfalls.action: On Windows do not chase Bun: disable the plugin and move on — in PowerShell, NOT inside Claude Code: `claude plugin disable claude-mem`. The hook does not affect the CLI. On Linux, installing Bun helps if you only see the (1) timeout: irm bun.sh/install.ps1 | iex (check: `where bun`). Do NOT rewrite the hook timeout in the plugin cache: the next update overwrites it.
known_pitfalls.note: 2026-09-02: on the laptop (Win11) the worker stayed unreachable even with the latest claude-mem (13.23.1), with Bun ALREADY PRESENT — this ruled out a missing runtime as the cause. On the VM (Linux, 13.23.0) it is flawless. On Windows disabling is the final answer, not a workaround. IMPORTANT: `claude plugin disable` only affects a NEW session — an already running session keeps running its own, previously loaded MCP server (node -e bootstrap + scripts/mcp-server.cjs from the plugin's .mcp.json). So after disabling, close the running sessions, otherwise you will think the disable did not work. On 2026-09-02 this is exactly what misled us.

known_pitfalls.when: After you added a new skill to the bajzi plugin
known_pitfalls.symptom: 'Unknown command' on the other machine, even though the marketplace was updated.
known_pitfalls.cause: `claude plugin update` looks at the version number. If the version in plugin.json and marketplace.json does not move, the update is a no-op.
known_pitfalls.action: ALWAYS bump the version in BOTH manifests (bajzi/.claude-plugin/plugin.json and .claude-plugin/marketplace.json), otherwise the change does not reach the other machines. The update takes effect at the next session start.

known_pitfalls.when: On a machine working with GSD
known_pitfalls.symptom: The ~4,270 token always-on cost is there even if you never use GSD in that repo.
known_pitfalls.cause: GSD's skills are machine-wide; .claude/METHODOLOGY controls WHAT THE MODEL USES, not WHAT GETS LOADED.
known_pitfalls.action: Cluster disabling: /gsd-surface disable <cluster>. Switching the base profile gives little (the full tier only adds 10 skills). Restore: /gsd-surface reset.

known_pitfalls.when: On any machine where rtk's PreToolUse hook is active (automatic rewriting of Bash commands)
known_pitfalls.symptom: When comparing two files, `diff A B` prints 'Files are identical' even though the files differ byte for byte; and `grep -h pattern f1 f2` over several files prints rtk grep's help text instead of the search result.
known_pitfalls.cause: The hook silently rewrites the Bash command into rtk's own compressing command (grep -> rtk grep, etc.), and the wrapper's output is not equivalent to the original: for diff it is not merely shorter, it states the OPPOSITE. This is a silent failure — nothing warns you that the command was rewritten.
known_pitfalls.action: Whenever a DECISION depends on the output (are two files identical, is there a match, what exactly changed), bypass the wrapper: `rtk proxy <command>` runs it raw, or use a command whose output cannot be mis-compressed (md5sum, `cmp -s`). Keep rtk for large, orientational output: build, test, lint, logs.
known_pitfalls.note: 2026-09-02: found while diffing the bajzi 1.5.4 -> 1.5.5 update. `diff -rq` still reported the difference correctly, but `diff` on the file pair said 'identical' while the md5 sums differed; only `rtk proxy diff` showed the real change.

known_pitfalls.when: Several Claude Code sessions are open on the same project at the same time (this is the normal case on the dev box)
known_pitfalls.symptom: A session's handover vanishes, or after /clear a session resumes a task it was never working on. Nothing is logged and nothing warns you.
known_pitfalls.cause: Before 1.5.8 both the /bajzi:handoff skill and the SessionStart hook used ONE hardcoded path per project, runtime/HANDOFF.md. Whoever closed out last overwrote everyone else, and the hook loaded that file for every session regardless of which task it belonged to.
known_pitfalls.action: From 1.5.8 handovers live at runtime/handoff/<branch-slug>.md, one per task, and the hook loads only the file matching the current branch. If no handover matches your task but others exist, the hook LISTS them and loads nothing on purpose — ask for one by name if you want it. Two sessions on the same branch are guarded by the Owner-session header: /bajzi:handoff asks before overwriting a file another session wrote in the last 2 hours.
known_pitfalls.note: 2026-09-02: the legacy runtime/HANDOFF.md path is still read, so nothing breaks on upgrade; the next /bajzi:handoff migrates it. Slug = branch name lowercased with everything outside [a-z0-9._-] turned into '-', truncated to 60 chars; anything git cannot answer (no repo, detached HEAD, dubious ownership) becomes 'default'.

known_pitfalls.when: Editing files in a checkout that has been sitting around for a while, especially one worktree among several for the same repo
known_pitfalls.symptom: The work is finished and committed, and only then does it turn out the base file was long obsolete — e.g. a CLAUDE.md translated from a 187-line version while the live one on origin/dev was 109 lines. A push is rejected non-fast-forward, or worse, succeeds and carries the stale content.
known_pitfalls.cause: git status, git log and ahead/behind counts all read remote-tracking refs, which go stale SILENTLY. A clean working tree says nothing about whether the tree matches the remote. Without a fetch the checkout can be hundreds of commits behind and still look perfectly healthy.
known_pitfalls.action: ALWAYS `git fetch` before judging git state or editing in a long-lived worktree. Then `git rev-list --left-right --count HEAD...origin/<branch>` (left = ahead, right = behind). If local commits look duplicated, `git cherry -v origin/<branch> HEAD` tells you whether dropping them loses anything: '-' = already upstream, '+' = unique to you.
known_pitfalls.note: 2026-09-02: found the hard way — a checkout 273 commits behind origin/dev produced three byte-identical translations of a file that had been rewritten 12 days earlier. The non-fast-forward rejection on one branch is what surfaced it; the branch that pushed cleanly needed a revert.

known_pitfalls.when: Releasing a new version of this plugin
known_pitfalls.symptom: The version is bumped and pushed, but on another machine `claude plugin update bajzi@bajzi-plugins` reports 'already up to date' and installs nothing — or the marketplace advertises a version that does not match what is actually shipped.
known_pitfalls.cause: There are TWO manifests and they are easy to desynchronize: bajzi/.claude-plugin/plugin.json (the plugin's own version) and .claude-plugin/marketplace.json (the version the marketplace advertises). 1.5.8 and 1.5.9 bumped only the first, leaving the marketplace entry at 1.5.7.
known_pitfalls.action: Bump BOTH in the same commit, then verify from the remote before telling anyone to update: `git show origin/main:.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`. Note that a stale marketplace entry does not necessarily block the update — on the dev box 1.5.7 -> 1.5.8 -> 1.5.9 all installed correctly while marketplace.json still said 1.5.7, because the version resolved from the plugin's own manifest via the './bajzi' source. Fix it regardless: the advertised version being wrong is a defect on its own.
known_pitfalls.note: 2026-09-02: caught by the laptop session during the 1.5.9 rollout, before anyone acted on the stale entry.

known_pitfalls.when: Git Bash on Windows, reading a file straight out of git
known_pitfalls.symptom: `git show "origin/main:.claude-plugin/marketplace.json"` fails with 'ambiguous argument', and it looks like the file is missing. Paths with more slashes (e.g. bajzi/.claude-plugin/plugin.json) work fine, so the failure looks selective and file-specific.
known_pitfalls.cause: MSYS path conversion rewrites the argument into 'origin\\main;.claude-plugin\\marketplace.json' before git ever sees it. Quoting does not help — the mangling happens in the MSYS layer, not the shell.
known_pitfalls.action: Prefix the command with MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1, e.g. `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 git show origin/main:path/to/file`.
known_pitfalls.note: 2026-09-02: reported by the laptop session. Only affects Git Bash on Windows; the Linux boxes are unaffected.

known_pitfalls.symptom: After a GSD update the always-on token count jumps and .env reads are no longer denied.
known_pitfalls.cause: 1.14 installs a skill dir for every command (45 duplicate names) and deletes the permissions.deny block that 1.12 wrote, replacing it with gsd-secret-read-guard.js.
known_pitfalls.fix: Follow gsd.after_every_update. Measured 2026-09-15 on the VM: raw 1.14 install = 46 skills + 46 commands + 29 agents; trimmed to 9 + 46 + 26 = ~3,019 always-on tokens.
known_pitfalls.also: Help text's --profile=core,audit is a trap: valid names are only core/standard/full, unknown tokens are dropped silently and --profile=audit alone falls back to FULL.
known_pitfalls.agents: Do NOT cut the agent layer to chase the old ~1,463 number — that number came from 1.12 staging no agents at all, i.e. broken dispatches.

known_pitfalls.status: RESOLVED in GSD 1.14.0 — kept for history
known_pitfalls.symptom: Statusline stuck on '⚠ stale hooks — run /gsd-update', and running /gsd-update never cleared it.
known_pitfalls.cause: gsd-check-update-worker.js marks any MANAGED_HOOKS file without a 'gsd-hook-version:' comment as stale; 1.12's gsd-node-runner.sh had none.
known_pitfalls.fix: Update to 1.14.0 — it ships the comment (verified: '# gsd-hook-version: 1.14.0'). The old hand-patch procedure is obsolete.

noise_filter.what: PreToolUse(Bash) hook in this plugin: hooks/noise-filter.sh + hooks/noise-run.sh. Keeps loud, low-information command output out of the context window.
noise_filter.mechanism: PostToolUse CANNOT shrink a tool result — it only ADDS text (additionalContext). Verified against the Claude Code 2.1.272 binary: 'updatedInput' 103 hits, 'updatedOutput' 0. So the rewrite must happen in PreToolUse via hookSpecificOutput.updatedInput.
noise_filter.exit_code: The runner never pipes the command into tail — a pipeline returns tail's status and a FAILED BUILD WOULD LOOK SUCCESSFUL. It captures to a log, then prints head + error lines + final summary, and exits with the original rc.
noise_filter.scope: Allowlist only: package installs and builds (npm/yarn/pnpm/bun, pip/uv, cargo/go, docker, apt, make/gradle/mvn, terraform init|plan). Anything under BAJZI_NOISE_KEEP (40) lines passes through whole. Output on failure is kept MORE, never less.
noise_filter.rtk_boundary: Complementary, not competing: pytest/ruff/git/ls/find/grep/`err npm run build` stay rtk's; commands already starting with `rtk` are skipped, so the two PreToolUse hooks never rewrite the same call.
noise_filter.measured: 2026-09-15, npm install --loglevel verbose: 28,295 -> 2,967 chars (-89.5%), rc preserved (0 on success, 1 on a failing pip install). NOTE: Claude Code runs Bash without a TTY, so many tools already suppress their progress bars — the real win is on verbose installs, builds and test runners, not on a plain `npm install`.
